In order for me to go from one level of my life to the next…

the version of health I want has to be greater than the comfort I’ve been settling for.

Humans don’t transition when they’re comfortable.

We only rise when we look at the level we’re on and finally say,
“Enough.”

I stopped eating from habits that kept me stuck.

I stopped living inside abandoned versions of myself.

I got tired — not of the work — but of the old level I owned.

That’s when the shift happens.

Some of us stay stuck because we get content.

Because being tired feels easier than being transformed.

But I’m done accepting the life that was handed to me.

I’m building the one I was meant to live —
through discipline, through sweat, through choosing myself again and again.

This is my next level.
#transformation

Never underestimate the people you say you care about.

Everyone carries a kind of power you can’t always see — emotional, intellectual, spiritual.

The moment you underestimate someone, you put yourself at a disadvantage.

This is why The Four Agreements matter:
✔️ Be impeccable with your word
✔️ Don’t take things personally
✔️ Don’t make assumptions
✔️ Always do your best

Respect isn’t weakness.
It’s awareness.
It’s alignment.
It’s strength.

Yesterday I talked about how underestimating people is the fastest way to fumble opportunities.

But here’s the twist I had to face myself…
the person I was underestimating the most was me.

All those little thoughts —
“I don’t look like them.”
“I don’t dress like them.”
“My life isn’t polished enough.”
That’s not humility.
That’s self-sabotage dressed up as realism.

If you said those things to someone else, they’d walk away.

So why speak to yourself like that?

This version of me is choosing to level up.

Choosing to believe I belong in the rooms I walk into.

Choosing to stop treating myself like the weakest character in my own video game.

Never underestimate the people around you.

But most importantly — never underestimate yourself.

Let’s embrace failure and transform one version at a time.

Still becoming.

I’m rehearsing for something amazing I’ve been secretly manifesting and telling only my closest friends about.

I take a few minutes to tune my nervous system.

Sound does something simple for me —
it slows me down.
It signals safety.

It helps my body move out of fight-or-flight and into rest, digest, and clarity.

I’m not trying to fix anything.
I’m just creating the conditions for balance.

When I start the day regulated,
my breath is deeper,
my reactions are softer, 
and my mind feels less crowded.

This is part of my daily maintenance —
like stretching, hydration, or silence.
A way to listen instead of rush.
To respond instead of react.

This is how I get out of bed now.
Tuned.
Present.
Clear enough to meet the day as it is.

I’ve been sitting with something lately.

In relational therapy, they talk about rupture and repair — the idea that it’s not the absence of failure that builds trust, intimacy, or growth… it’s what we do after we fall on our face.

Angela Duckworth calls it GRIT: passion + perseverance over time. Not perfection. Not talent. Time in the arena. Time eating a little dirt.

Failure isn’t a verdict.
It’s feedback.
It’s information.
It’s the place where we finally stop performing and start becoming.

When things fall apart, there’s always a fifty percent we bring to the table. 

That’s not blame — that’s power. That’s agency. That’s where growth lives.

And here’s the part we don’t talk about enough — FAILURE can actually bring JOY.

Not because it feels good in the moment — but because it carries anticipation.

Anticipation that you’re learning.
Anticipation that you’re getting closer.
Anticipation that this version of you won’t be the final release.

So fail fast.
Fail honestly.
Fail with curiosity instead of shame.

Then repair.
Refactor.

And release the next iteration of yourself — a little more grounded, a little more resilient, a little more you.

I’m rooting for you. Always.

I’ve been craving this for a while.
The edge between heat and cold.
Fire and snow.
Presence and risk.

Today isn’t about performance.
It’s about being in my body long enough to hear what it’s been trying to say.

I’m building the fire.
The ritual comes next.

Because no one else can give the world your presence.

The holidays can quietly turn us into servants of love—
meeting needs, fulfilling wishes, holding space, making everyone else smile.

And there’s real joy in that. Dopamine. Purpose. Belonging.

But this year, I’m choosing something just as sacred.

Time to enjoy myself.
My creativity.
My imagination.

The silly, vibrant, sexy world I once only carried in my head.

This Christmas, I’m practicing something radical and gentle — seeing myself not as what I give away—but as what I bring.

So today, I wrapped myself as a reminder:
I matter. My presence matters. I am the gift.

And if you’re watching this—
I hope you try it on too.

One of the most romantic things you can do is live long enough to love someone for the full arc.

Nobody talks about longevity inside relationships. 

We talk about chemistry, timing, values, sex, aesthetics — but the quiet question underneath is:

Can we make it long enough to enjoy the whole thing?

As we get older we start thinking about care, decline, and logistics. We watch parents lose mobility, lose memory, lose dignity, and we realize how physical partnership really is.

You don’t have to be a “hottie,” but longevity requires honoring your body together. 

Muscle mass, VO₂ max, metabolic health, and social bonds are all survival variables after 60.

Harvard’s 85-year study found that relationships were the strongest predictor of healthy aging. 

Gerontologists call it health concordance — couples literally age in parallel.

If I want to love you until 70+ years old, I need this body to serve, carry, play, hold, and remember.

I want to live long so I can love long.

How long do you want to go?

#longevity #healthspan #relationships #agingwell fitat50

Why I wander before dawn. 

Most people only experience certain spaces at peak volume — packed with bodies, noise, urgency, and expectation. 

I love those moments too, but my secret joy has always happened in the hours before all of that arrives.

Early mornings in places built for thousands feel almost sacred. 

Without the crowds, I get to witness the architecture, the light, the echoes, the quiet logic of how a place is designed to serve human life. 

You can’t notice any of that when the space is doing its job at full capacity.

Having it to myself gives me room to reflect, to show gratitude, and to pause inside a world that rarely slows down on its own. 

It’s where I reorganize my thoughts, check in with my values, and remember what matters to me before the day starts making demands.

It’s a small ritual — one I hope to never stop doing — and honestly it’s been one of the greatest blessings I’ve been given. 

The world feels chaotic, but these quiet moments remind me I still get to choose how I enter it.

Day 14 of 30 — I’m realizing most of the handstand happens before the handstand.

The bottleneck isn’t strength, it’s mobility and nervous system control. 

So today was shoulder + thoracic opening, long holds (30–60s), and a final set to failure to see where the edge actually is.

Inverted stability work (pike push-ups + vibration plates) continues to be the real cheat code. 

It forces everything to organize while upside down.

The trick is just the celebration. The preparation is the transformation.

For most of my life I thought about the body in terms of muscles, emotions, or stress.

But underneath all of that we’re electrical systems.

Every cell runs on voltage.
Every emotion has a frequency.
Change the input → the system changes.

What people call “chakras,” I’m approaching as seven energy nodes in a closed electrical circuit. More functional than mystical.

So before I started working with them, I ran an AO scan — basically a frequency assessment that shows where my system is overcharged, undercharged, or out of resonance.

This became my baseline.

From here, the experiment begins:
→  identify missing frequencies
→  counteract through light, sound, color, voice, & environment
→  observe how behavior outputs change
→  repeat daily

Some days I need confidence.
Some days I need grounding.
Some days I need expression.
Every day is different.

I’m wired for systems, details, iteration — for noticing how tiny adjustments change the entire experience of a thing.

The walk.
The carriage of the shoulders.
The architecture of a pose.
The strange engineering of confidence, timing, tension, release.

What surprised me most about the 2026 Makers Way Runway Show wasn’t the fashion.

It was discovering a local community that approaches presence the way makers approach craft — through experimentation, observation, play, repetition, and an almost irrational devotion to nuance.

Practicing with friends.
Geeking out over movement.
Refining the nearly invisible details most people would never notice.

Some may call it performative.

Maybe.

But so is music. 🎼
So is dance.💃 
So is design. 💻

So is every art form that asks us to intentionally shape how an experience is felt.

Runway, I’ve learned, is not just something you do.

It’s something you build.

Runway is a Makers Way.

Years of loving people with different attachment styles have taught me one thing: reciprocal curiosity is far more valuable than labels.

TL; DR;
I’ve loved someone who was strongly dismissive avoidant. I spent years with someone who was fearful avoidant. More recently, I’ve experienced a relationship with someone who leaned more anxious.

I’m an extremely curious person, so navigating these dynamics has become a lifelong research project, one I’m not sure I’ll ever master.

Ironically, those relationships helped me realize something about myself. I feel fundamentally secure. 

Not because I never get anxious or always know the right thing to say.

Typically, the opposite but because I’ve learned to recognize my own reflections in the people I have fallen in love with.

What I’ve learned is that attachment theory isn’t about labeling people. It’s about becoming curious.

To me, emotional intelligence is understanding yourself without abandoning yourself, while creating enough safety for someone else to do the same.

Note to my future self:

When you meet someone, learn what closeness means to them. Learn what makes them feel safe. Learn what makes them withdraw.

Not to manage them, but so you can understand them.

At the same time, don’t lose yourself trying to earn someone’s love. If someone isn’t curious about what hurts you, pay attention to their actions.

Do they ask how you feel?

Do they communicate their boundaries?

Can you stay emotionally regulated together when conversations become difficult?

Do you feel warm? Invited? Safe enough to be your authentic self?

Or do you feel like you’re constantly trying to be chosen?

If it isn’t aligned, it doesn’t have to become complicated. Keep it simple. Stay curious. Let trust develop at a pace that feels safe for both of you.

Say the words out loud. Be authentic. Trust that your authentic self is worthy of being loved exactly as it is.

Love people where they’re at, but don’t abandon where you are while you’re doing it.

Look for your own reflection in the mirror.
